question: Right after a disaster strikes, what is the main thing nurses and responders focus on first?

options.B: Protecting human life and stabilizing the injured
options.D: Providing financial loans to displaced families

explanation: When an emergency hits, your immediate priority as a nurse is always saving lives and keeping people stable before worrying about anything else. You've got this! [learn more](GNS315_U5_T5#GNS315_U5_T5_h1)

question: How does your job as a nurse change when you step out of a normal hospital and into a disaster zone?

options.A: The nurse only focuses on administrative paperwork
options.B: The nurse must rely more on quick improvisations and resource-scarce settings
options.C: The nurse works exclusively with advanced robotic surgical tools
options.D: The nurse stops providing direct patient care entirely

explanation: Disasters mess up normal hospital supplies, so you'll often have to think on your feet and make the best of what's available around you. It's tough, but Nigerian nurses do it brilliantly! [learn more](GNS315_U5_T5#GNS315_U5_T5_h1)

question: During triage at a disaster scene, which color tag goes to patients who can walk and only have minor cuts or scrapes?
explanation: Think of 'Green' like a green light—these are the walking wounded who are stable and don't need emergency rushing to the theatre. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T5#GNS315_U5_T5_h2)

question: A patient tagged as yellow suddenly starts gasping for air and showing signs of shock. What should you do?

options.A: Ask the patient to walk over to the green area
options.B: Leave the patient in the yellow category because triage tags never change
options.C: Re-tag the patient as red and provide immediate life-saving care
options.D: Move the patient to the black category immediately

explanation: Triage isn't a one-time thing; patient conditions change fast! If someone gets worse, you upgrade their tag right away to get them urgent help. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T5#GNS315_U5_T5_h2)

question: When setting up a temporary camp for people displaced by a disaster, which type of location should you strictly avoid?

options.A: Flat land with easy access to roads
options.B: Areas far away from stagnant water bodies
options.C: Locations with proper ventilation and spacing

explanation: Putting a camp in a swampy or flood-prone area just invites another disaster. Always look for high, safe ground! [learn more](GNS315_U5_T5#GNS315_U5_T5_h3)

question: Why is it so important to leave enough space between tents when setting up a temporary disaster camp?

options.A: It helps prevent the rapid spread of airborne and contact illnesses
options.B: It ensures everyone gets the exact same size tent
options.C: It makes the camp look more organized for visitors
options.D: It allows heavy machinery to drive through the tents at night

explanation: When people are packed too tightly together, illnesses like coughs and infections spread like wildfire. Space keeps everyone safer! [learn more](GNS315_U5_T5#GNS315_U5_T5_h3)

question: What major health threat usually pops up first when clean water supplies and sewage systems break down during a disaster?
explanation: When sewage mixes with drinking water, tummy troubles and deadly infections like cholera follow fast. Safe water is lifesaving! [learn more](GNS315_U5_T5#GNS315_U5_T5_h4)

question: Why do emergency planners insist that temporary latrines must be built downhill and far away from community water sources?

options.A: To ensure the smell blows away from the tents
options.B: To prevent sewage from contaminating the community's drinking water supply
options.C: To keep the ground dry and prevent mud
options.D: To make them easier to clean with heavy machinery

explanation: Gravity makes liquid flow downhill. If toilets are uphill from wells or streams, waste will wash straight into the drinking water. Basic hygiene logic! [learn more](GNS315_U5_T5#GNS315_U5_T5_h4)

question: Which simple tool do nurses use right in the field to quickly check if a child is suffering from malnutrition?
explanation: The colorful MUAC tape is a nurse's best friend in community outreaches and disaster zones for spotting malnutrition in seconds. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T5#GNS315_U5_T5_h5)

question: Why are Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Foods (RUTF) so popular for feeding hungry children early in a disaster?

options.A: They have a very short shelf life that forces quick consumption
options.B: They taste sweet and only appeal to adults
options.C: They provide quick nutrition without needing clean cooking water or fuel
options.D: They replace the need for breastfeeding entirely

explanation: When there's no firewood or clean water to cook with, RUTF packets save the day by providing instant, safe nourishment. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T5#GNS315_U5_T5_h5)

question: What is a common, dangerous mistake when handing out crutches or walking sticks to injured people in a disaster?

options.A: Ensuring they match the person's height
options.B: Cleaning them with soap and water before use
options.C: Giving them out without proper physical fitting and instruction
options.D: Storing them in dry storage tents

explanation: Crutches that are too tall or too short can cause nasty falls or nerve injuries. Always fit assistive devices properly to the patient! [learn more](GNS315_U5_T5#GNS315_U5_T5_h6)

question: Why is clearing away rubble and setting up temporary ramps so vital inside a disaster relief camp?

options.A: It helps people with mobility challenges move safely around the camp
options.B: It replaces the need for medical triage stations
options.C: It completely stops the spread of waterborne diseases
options.D: It is required before anyone is allowed to eat

explanation: Debris blocks pathways, making life impossible for wheelchair users or the elderly. Ramps and clear paths bring back their independence. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T5#GNS315_U5_T5_h6)

question: Which common insect breeds like crazy in stagnant floodwaters after heavy rains or a disaster?
explanation: Still floodwaters are breeding paradises for mosquitoes, driving up malaria risks. Netting and draining standing water are key nursing interventions! [learn more](GNS315_U5_T5#GNS315_U5_T5_h7)

question: Why must used needles and medical waste be disposed of with extreme care in a disaster camp?

options.A: To provide building materials for temporary shelters
options.B: To make the garbage bags look neat and tidy
options.C: To keep the air smelling fresh for the residents
options.D: To prevent accidental needle-stick injuries and biological contamination

explanation: Throwing sharps around carelessly can easily injure children playing nearby or fellow health workers. Safety first, always! [learn more](GNS315_U5_T5#GNS315_U5_T5_h7)

question: What is one of the biggest physical dangers people with chronic illnesses face when they have to evacuate in a hurry?

options.A: Gaining too much weight from inactivity

explanation: In a sudden rush to escape, patients often leave behind their blood pressure or diabetes drugs. Nurses must check for this early! [learn more](GNS315_U5_T5#GNS315_U5_T5_h8)

question: Why do disaster coordinators try to house elderly or chronically ill patients close to the main medical tents?

options.A: To isolate them completely from the rest of the community
options.B: To allow for quicker response if their health condition suddenly deteriorates
options.C: To make it easier for them to clean the medical equipment
options.D: To reduce the walking distance for medical staff delivering food

explanation: Vulnerable patients can crash quickly in emergencies. Keeping them close to medical help means doctors and nurses can reach them in seconds. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T5#GNS315_U5_T5_h8)
